articles.title: JD Vance is right: Foreign policy lost the election
articles.summary: Trump’s ill-fated adventure in Iran has shown voters that American power projection abroad comes at a high cost.
articles.body:
The morning after the elections, JD Vance delivered a stunning rebuke to the sitting president by way of a tweet : “The reason we lost is the war.” As a general rule, foreign policy does not decide the outcome of U.S. elections. This time was different.

In early 2026, things were not looking too bad for the Republican Party. Forty-one percent of Americans still viewed President Trump favorably, and betting markets solidly predicted a Republican victory in the Senate. But as the war started and gas prices went up, Trump’s approval ratings plummeted to historic lows . Trump urged Americans to vote as though the president himself was on the ballot — and they did.

In post-election surveys, few voters cited foreign policy as the primary issue of this election. Among the most important issues facing the country, foreign policy featured a distant fifth behind the economy at 39 percent, democracy at 32 percent, immigration at 14 percent and healthcare at 8 percent.

But it is clear that inflation and high gas prices — the drivers of the country’s economic woes — are a direct consequence of Trump’s war in Iran. Moody’s estimated recently that the conflict has cost American households an average of $2,000. This fact was not lost on voters; three-fourths of whom said the Iran war was a major or crucial factor in their voting choice.

A number of other hot-button campaign issues turned out to be less important. Tariffs and trade wars affect the Midwest most strongly, and yet Democrats comparatively underperformed in Michigan, Minnesota and Ohio. Data centers are similarly unpopular; still, young voters — the demographic that shifted most to the left — cared least about the issue.

In a similar vein, the shift among Latino voters seems almost entirely driven by the rising cost of living and not — as some analysts were quick to conclude — immigration. In a September poll , Latino voters were split over which party to trust with the border; the share of Latinos that believe Democrats are better at “dealing with immigration” has barely moved since 2022.

Meanwhile, it was particularly young Republicans and independents that repudiated the president’s interventionist legacy. Seven in 10 Gen Z voters turned out for Democrats, a more than 30-point shift from 2024. This intra-party rebellion has been months in the making. An April poll found that strong majorities of older conservatives strongly supported the president’s actions in Iran, compared to only 28 percent of those 18 to 34. The same is true of Israel, where 72 percent of Gen Z Republicans oppose Trump’s unconditional support.

Even Trump himself has seen the writing on the wall. In a last-ditch attempt on Election Day — incongruously accompanied by another airstrike on Iran — President Trump announced he would discontinue military aid to Israel by year’s end. The morning after Election Day, his vice president said Republicans would need to do at least four things to bring their lost voters back into the fold: end the war, focus on inflation, put America first and change the U.S.-Israel relationship.

Of course, Vance — who appears willing to risk Trump’s endorsement with such scathing criticism — is already setting himself up for the next presidential cycle. But it is worth considering what the recent results will mean for that campaign.

After Trump’s betrayal of “ no new wars ,” the Republican base is unlikely to give another mandate to a neoconservative, or anyone tainted by the disastrous Iran war. And it would have been unimaginable until very recently for a Republican frontrunner to openly call for a reversal of the GOP’s alliance with Israel.

The same, of course, is true of the left, where Gaza has become a litmus test for a party base still furious over the Biden administration’s handling of Israel. Even presidential hopeful Rahm Emanuel, who once volunteered with the Israel Defense Forces, has called for an end to arms sales to Israel earlier this year. Though avowed Israel critics like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed or Maine’s Troy Jackson still faced an uphill battle with the party establishment, the issue may be one of style rather than substance.

In the near term, it is difficult to predict how Trump will respond to his voters’ rejection of his foreign policy. He may attempt to salvage his legacy by scrambling for a settlement with Iran and belatedly turning on Israel. Or, Trump, a lame-duck president with a domestic agenda now imperiled by looming internecine insurgencies and scuttled by congressional subpoenas, may double down on an increasingly delusional expansionist vision encompassing Cuba to Iran.

In the long term, the midterm results will accelerate a belated reckoning about America’s diminished role in the world. Trump’s ill-fated adventure in Iran has shown voters that American power projection abroad comes at a high cost. Foreign policy may not be an election winner — but it can certainly lose one.

Johannes Lang is an AI researcher and McCain Global Leader focusing on the domestic politics of U.S. foreign policy.

articles.title: The midterms gave Congress a mandate — now use it
articles.summary: Following recent elections, the McCain Institute urges Congress to embrace bipartisan leadership to address economic pressures, regulate emerging technologies like AI, and strengthen global security against adversaries like Russia and China.
articles.body:
The American people have spoken through the ballot box. They have repudiated the war on Iran and other misguided policies and made clear they want leaders who understand and tackle the most important problems while treating their fellow Americans with human dignity and fairness. They seek leaders with character and integrity, who refuse to stoop to fear-mongering and derision, leaders like the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) who famously pushed back at a public town hall in 2008 when a supporter attempted to smear his White House opponent, then-Sen. Barack Obama (D-Ill.).

American voters picked candidates who they felt understood the challenges facing working families and have the experience and determination to address them. They voted for a return to an America where the demands of the working and middle class dictate politics, not the money and power wielded by a handful of politically connected billionaires. Ultimately, consciously or not, they voted for a government that will work in a bipartisan fashion to forge consensus and pass smart legislation.

Congress now has an opportunity to lean into bipartisan problem-solving, to enact bipartisan foreign and domestic policies to address economic and fiscal pressures. Congress must address the president’s overreach on tariffs and take other steps to better manage the economy and address voter grievances.

At the same time, Congress must authorize and fund a defense and foreign policy to keep America out of war — by boosting our defense deterrence, strengthening security alliances and foreign partnerships, harnessing technology and American innovation. A strong defense will advance U.S. economic interests and vice versa. Nonetheless, there will be constraints. To balance budget discipline with necessary spending will require smart, courageous leadership.

For almost a decade and a half, our organization has regularly convened members of Congress from both parties, Cabinet officials, foreign heads of state, CEOs, political dissidents and other global leaders to address difficult national and international security issues.

They examine issues such as the impact of technology on modern warfare, how to counter Chinese activities in Africa and Latin America and Russia’s imperial and brutal foreign policy, how to strengthen our security alliances and how to support leaders in Venezuela and around the world who are fighting for human rights and democracy. At our signature Sedona Forum and beyond, we highlight and supports the actions of courageous leaders and connects them with one another.

As we finish this year and move into 2027, we will lean into our bipartisanship and convene small and large gatherings to help members of Congress and other policymakers advance an agenda that supports robust U.S. engagement around the world to advance our interests and values. We must work with public and private stakeholders to ensure that AI is shaped and utilized in a way that conforms with our democratic values — freedom, transparency — and keeps America secure and in the lead, particularly against China and other adversaries.

We must revamp our conventional deterrence to be a more agile mix of high and low technology and density assets and maintain our strategic nuclear deterrence, even while we remain alert to opportunities to negotiate verifiable arms control. We must encourage our allies as they increase their defense capabilities, and we must cooperate to bolster allied, and Ukrainian, industrial synergies, secure supply chains and ultimately fortify our collective defense.

Immediate next steps for Congress during the lame duck session should include reasserting its role on tariff and sanctions policy, specifically in the latter case, with regard to Russia. Congress should demand laws be enforced, starting with the sanctions bill named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The law requires the administration to provide written justification for the waiver the White House recently declared in order to purchase diesel from Moscow. Congress must demand this and then repudiate it declaratively, if not legislatively. Even the declaration will add to the legal uncertainties for any port or business entities considering offloading and distributing this figuratively blood-soaked fuel.

Our national security clearly demands the swiftest, durable end to Russia’s war of aggression in order to restore security and international law in Europe and beyond, deter China from further aggressive action in the South China Sea or against Taiwan, and restore U.S. defense stockpiles. The only way to do this is to squeeze Russia’s access to capital, technology and hardware to supply its war effort.

The risks to U.S. interests have grown with the escalatory Russian attacks on European territory over the last four years — culminating recently in two ships being sunk by Russia off the coast of Bulgaria and armed drones flying to an airport in Leipzig, Germany . These terrorist acts are dangerous and could lead to military clashes between Russia and NATO. To stop Russia from continued escalation, we must work with our allies to pressure Vladimir Putin to realize that he must negotiate a real end to the war.

Congress can also start drafting legislation on social media and AI that would balance protecting our democratic values, freedom, privacy and safety with the need to reap advantages and maintain a global competitive edge. On the international front, this would include encouraging the administration to work with China on international rules that would protect humanity from the worst-case scenarios. The lame-duck Congress can quickly assert its intent on sanctions and other issues where there is already consensus through bill and report language it will approve before January as part of the annual defense authorization bill.

Congress has the opportunity now to demonstrate character, courage and bipartisan leadership, drawing inspiration from the McCain’s career. After all, it was during his time as a statesman in Congress that McCain first developed his global reputation for character-driven leadership. And it was in his defeat as a presidential candidate 18 years ago this week that he declared: “Americans never quit. We never surrender. We never hide from history. We make history.” The elections are just the beginning of this next phase of history — which can and must be marked by a new burst of bipartisanship.

Evelyn N. Farkas, Ph.D., is executive director of the McCain Institute and former deputy assistant secretary of Defense.

articles.title: Makers of GLP-1 drugs ordered to add warnings about rare eye condition that can lead to blindness
articles.summary: The US Food and Drug Administration says Ozempic, Wegovy, and other weight-loss drugs must have labels about the condition, known as NAION.
articles.body:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) told makers of popular weight-loss GLP-1 drugs that they must add warning labels about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness.

Manufacturers of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound must warn about nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The disorder happens when vessels supplying blood to the optic nerves become blocked, depriving the nerves of oxygen.

The condition can cause painless decreased vision in one eye, which can be permanent, the FDA said.

In a statement to the BBC, the American Academy of Ophthalmology said "any added risk appears small, and it has not been established that these medications cause NAION".

"GLP-1 medications offer important benefits for people with diabetes, obesity, and heart disease, so our message to patients is simple," the group said. "Don't stop your medication without talking to your doctor, and if you notice sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, see an ophthalmologist promptly."

There is no known treatment to reverse vision loss caused by NAION. It is the most common cause of acute optic nerve injury in people over 50 years old, according to the academy.

The FDA said it conducted a detailed review of reports of NAION in GLP-1 users as well as a review of other studies and concluded there is an "increased risk of rare NAION events" in people taking the drugs.

In a statement, Novo Nordisk, the manufacturer of Wegovy, one of the most popular weight-loss medications, said the company believes the data "do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship".

"We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families. Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines," the manufacturer said.

Some research was challenging to review because people taking GLP-1 drugs for obesity and type 2 diabetes may already have risk factors for NAION separate from the drugs, according to the regulator. The FDA said it was not known why those taking GLP-1 drugs may be more at risk for the eye condition.

The drugs already have warning labels for several other conditions including pancreatitis and gallbladder disease. Some of the most common symptoms for semaglutide - a key ingredient in many GLP-1 drugs - include nausea, vomiting and stomach pain.

⁠Last year, a safety arm of the European Medicines Agency, a part of the European Union, said up to 1 in 10,000 people taking semaglutide may be affected by NAION.

In a study published two years ago analysing 17,000 patients, US researchers found those taking semaglutide were four times more likely to be diagnosed with NAION than those not taking the drug.

But one of the authors of the study, Harvard Medical School ophthalmology professor Dr Joseph Rizzo, said the findings were "significant but tentative", and more research was needed on the relationship between the drug and the eye condition in a more diverse population.

articles.title: US soldier suspected of Russia-related espionage arrested in UK
articles.summary: An unnamed U.S. Army soldier was arrested on Tuesday in the United Kingdom following an investigation into allegations of espionage related to Russia, according to British authorities. The Metropolitan Police said in a news release that the 41-year-old soldier is accused of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023, including obtaining or disclosing…
articles.body:
An unnamed U.S. Army soldier was arrested on Tuesday in the United Kingdom following an investigation into allegations of espionage related to Russia, according to British authorities.

The Metropolitan Police said in a news release that the 41-year-old soldier is accused of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023 , including obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a provided statement. “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

The soldier was taken into custody near Gloucester and remained at a London police station as of about 6:45 p.m. local time, according to the release. Authorities were also searching two locations in Gloucestershire, a county in southwestern England.

The release contained few details, with the commanding general of the U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command describing the individual only as a “senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information” whose conduct is a “sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”

“I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office,” Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon said in a statement.

Officials said the investigation was not linked to any other counterterrorism probes and was conducted in “close collaboration” with U.S. authorities.

“The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing,” said Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for the UK police’s counterterrorism network. “This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved.”

The FBI has made 167 counterintelligence and espionage-related arrests in the last 21 months, according to Patel.
